label: Beef consumption per inhabitant, kilograms
curated_subtitle: Beef per inhabitant, kilograms, 1935, by province
source_documents: Dirección General de Estadística. 1936. Anuario Estadístico de Chile, año 1935, livestock slaughtered by province. Santiago.
source_document: Anuario Estadístico de Chile, 1935 (livestock, province level)
definition: Kilograms of beef per inhabitant by province, 1935. It does NOT reconcile to the beef tonnage divided by the provincial population printed in the same table, agreeing for only twelve of nineteen provinces, so the source is using a different base or accounting for meat moved between provinces. Slaughter is recorded where the animal was killed, not where the meat was eaten, which makes this a measure of provincial slaughter capacity as much as of provincial diet.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)

The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.

breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

definition: Population of the urban centre itself at the census years 1875 to 1930, taken from the census volumes rather than reconstructed. breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

breaks.label: CONARA regionalization (13 regions replace provinces)
breaks.description: Decreto-Ley 575 of July 1974, implemented through 1975-1976, replaced Chile's 25-province structure with 13 regions plus the Metropolitan Region. Department-level reporting effectively ends; from this date forward the canonical subnational geography is the region (XV regions today, after later subdivisions).
breaks.citation: Decreto-Ley 575 de 1974; ODEPLAN/CONARA (1976), Chile hacia un nuevo destino.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Department and province series should not be drawn past 1974 without a notice; the data after this date originates from region-level reporting back-cast to the older units, which is interpolation. Recommended: terminate department/province series at 1973 by default with an option to view the back-cast extension.

breaks.label: SNEC professionalizes census-taking
breaks.description: The Servicio Nacional de Estadística y Censos (SNEC), created in 1953, professionalized the Chilean census. The 1952 census was the last under the older agency; from 1960 forward, census enumeration follows modernized UN-standard methodology.
breaks.citation: Ley 11,237 de 1953, creación del Servicio Nacional de Estadística y Censos.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Source caption flags the 1952-vs-1960 transition. No rule line; the discontinuity is in methodology, not in the data shape.

breaks.label: September 1973 — political rupture
breaks.description: The military government that took power on September 11, 1973 disrupted civilian statistical reporting for several years and introduced methodological changes in social and economic series. Fiscal, labor, and social-sector series across 1972–1976 are particularly affected by definitional turnover and, in some cases, political contestation of the published figures.
breaks.citation: Meller (2000); Ffrench-Davis (2001).
breaks.rule_for_chart: Light vertical rule at 1973 on long-run series. Tooltip notes the political-economic discontinuity without making a substantive judgment. Comparison across this break is methodologically legitimate but readers should know the regime change.

definition: Average daily attendance at the boys' liceo of each town, 1900 to 1909, from the Anuario Estadístico de Chile 1909. Read it against the matrícula series rather than alone: enrolment measures how many families put a son on the roll and attendance measures how many actually came, and the gap between them, roughly a quarter at the median, is the more informative quantity. The unit is the establishment, so a town with two liceos is not comparable to one with a single larger school.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

source_document: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional, Legislators Database
definition: Number of legislators (diputados plus senadores) representing the electoral district, Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional database, sampled at decade years. The data is stored at its as-printed constituency level, and the curated download ships it that way; the department map projects each district onto its department, which is valid before 1891 because electoral districts coincided with departments until the Ley de Comuna Autónoma reorganization. A district spanning several departments (for example Ancud y Quinchao) is never split across them and does not appear on the map; its rows remain in the download at constituency level. The 19th-century Chilean Congress had a small number of legislators per electoral district; counts of one or two were typical.

breaks.label: September 1973 — political rupture
breaks.description: The military government that took power on September 11, 1973 disrupted civilian statistical reporting for several years and introduced methodological changes in social and economic series. Fiscal, labor, and social-sector series across 1972–1976 are particularly affected by definitional turnover and, in some cases, political contestation of the published figures.
breaks.citation: Meller (2000); Ffrench-Davis (2001).
breaks.rule_for_chart: Light vertical rule at 1973 on long-run series. Tooltip notes the political-economic discontinuity without making a substantive judgment. Comparison across this break is methodologically legitimate but readers should know the regime change.

breaks.label: Unemployment series redefined (ENE)

source_document: Mamalakis, Markos. 1980. Historical Statistics of Chile, Vol. 2
definition: Total population of the unit (national, province, or department), the canonical population indicator at each scale. The national series is a continuous annual line of intercensal estimates; census enumerations are published alongside it as the separate indicator Total population (census enumerations), because an enumerated count and a mid-year estimate measure population on different definitions and can differ by several percent in the same year. The subnational series stitch together census enumerations (1865, 1875, 1885, 1895, 1907, 1920, 1930, 1940, 1952, 1960, 1970, 1982, 1992), Mamalakis (1980) intercensal estimates, and the Véjares department-level extraction. Earlier duplicate population series have been consolidated into this indicator. The annual national line is extracted as printed from Mamalakis (1980) Volume 2, Table 1.1 (page 4): June-30 estimates by the INE Section of Analysis and Measurement of Population, computed by geometric intercensal interpolation between census anchors, published in thousands and scaled to persons. Census-year values in that table follow the INE revised basis (its note 3 excludes territories not under effective Chilean sovereignty from the 1885, 1895, 1907, and 1920 censuses), so they can differ from the raw enumerations by up to several percent; values from 1976 onward are the INE projection series printed with the table. Every rendered value is a row in the curated download under source Mamalakis Vol 2, Table 1.1 (DEC/INE/ODEPLAN).
coverage_statement: 113 year(s) 1835-1992, 113 national observations; 16 year(s) 1843-1970, 315 province-level observations; 5 year(s) 1843-1878, 112 department-level observations; 3 year(s) 1935-1992, 798 observations

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

breaks.label: Tacna returned to Peru (Treaty of Lima)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Lima of June 3, 1929 settled the Tacna-Arica question: Tacna returned to Peru, Arica confirmed Chilean. National-aggregate series experience a small reduction in 1929; the Tacna department disappears from Chilean reporting after this date.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Lima, June 3, 1929; St. John (1992), The Bolivia–Chile–Peru Dispute.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1929 on national series with subnational composition. Department-level series for Tacna terminate in 1929 and should not be drawn beyond that year.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.

breaks.label: CONARA regionalization (13 regions replace provinces)
breaks.description: Decreto-Ley 575 of July 1974, implemented through 1975-1976, replaced Chile's 25-province structure with 13 regions plus the Metropolitan Region. Department-level reporting effectively ends; from this date forward the canonical subnational geography is the region (XV regions today, after later subdivisions).
breaks.citation: Decreto-Ley 575 de 1974; ODEPLAN/CONARA (1976), Chile hacia un nuevo destino.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Department and province series should not be drawn past 1974 without a notice; the data after this date originates from region-level reporting back-cast to the older units, which is interpolation. Recommended: terminate department/province series at 1973 by default with an option to view the back-cast extension.

breaks.label: SNEC professionalizes census-taking

breaks.label: September 1973 — political rupture

breaks.label: Decimal peso introduced
breaks.description: Chile decimalized its currency, replacing the colonial real-based system with a peso of 100 centavos. Pre-1851 fiscal series originate in reales and were converted to pesos at the source; conversions are not always documented per cell.
breaks.citation: Decreto sobre Monedas, 9 de enero de 1851; Banco Central de Chile, Historia Monetaria de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a thin vertical rule at 1851 on any nominal-peso series. Hover tooltip names the reform. Do not gray; the conversion is per-cell at the source.

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

source_document: Sinopsis Estadística i Jeográfica de Chile (19th c.)
definition: Expenditure by the Ministerio de Guerra as a percentage of total fiscal spending, at thirteen benchmark years from 1842 to 1900. This is the largest single head in the early series and the one that moves most: it opens at 35.2% in 1842, when the army still absorbed more than a third of the budget, and falls steadily as instruction, public works and colonisation claim shares of their own. Read it together with the Navy and Treasury heads rather than alone, since the eleven ministry shares are a closed decomposition and sum to 100% in ten of the thirteen years; the remaining three miss by between 0.02 and 3.0 points, which is printed rounding and a small head the source omits, not a gap in the data.

display_label: Expenditure on the Navy as % of total fiscal spending
curated_subtitle: Navy ministry share of fiscal spending, 1842–1900, %
source_documents: Oficina Central de Estadística. ca. 1858. Sinopsis Estadística i Jeográfica de la República de Chile. Santiago: Imprenta Nacional.
source_document: Sinopsis Estadística i Jeográfica de Chile (19th c.)
definition: Expenditure by the Ministerio de Marina as a percentage of total fiscal spending, at thirteen benchmark years from 1842 to 1900. The naval share is the one place in the budget where the War of the Pacific is legible: Chile fought it at sea first, and the series carries the build-up and the subsequent settling. The Navy is reported separately from War throughout, so the two must be added to recover total military spending; neither is a complete measure of it on its own.

source_document: Sinopsis Estadística i Jeográfica de Chile (19th c.)
definition: Expenditure by the Ministerio de Hacienda as a percentage of total fiscal spending, at thirteen benchmark years from 1842 to 1900. The head is larger than a finance ministry would suggest to a modern reader, 42.2% in 1842, because it carries debt service and the customs administration alongside the ministry's own costs. It is therefore a poor proxy for bureaucratic size and a good one for the weight of borrowing and of the customs house in nineteenth-century Chilean public finance.

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

breaks.label: Tacna returned to Peru (Treaty of Lima)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Lima of June 3, 1929 settled the Tacna-Arica question: Tacna returned to Peru, Arica confirmed Chilean. National-aggregate series experience a small reduction in 1929; the Tacna department disappears from Chilean reporting after this date.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Lima, June 3, 1929; St. John (1992), The Bolivia–Chile–Peru Dispute.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1929 on national series with subnational composition. Department-level series for Tacna terminate in 1929 and should not be drawn beyond that year.

breaks.label: Anuario primary → later compiled official series
breaks.description: For long-run national series (GDP, fiscal aggregates, foreign trade, demographics), the pre-1929 segment is drawn from the primary archival series (Anuario Estadistico, Sinopsis, Memoria), while later years rely on subsequent official statistical series. Definitions were harmonized across the join and may differ slightly from the original primary readings.
breaks.citation: Primary Chilean statistical series (Anuario, Sinopsis, Memoria) and later official series.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Source caption attributes by year-segment per audit Finding 4.2. No vertical rule required unless a definitional revision crossed this date.

breaks.citation: Decreto sobre Monedas, 9 de enero de 1851; Banco Central de Chile, Historia Monetaria de Chile.

definition: Total ordinary revenue of the Chilean treasury from 1833 to 1914, as compiled by Aldana in 1914 from the annual accounts. The series spans the shift from a customs based revenue system to one dominated by the nitrate export duty after 1880, which is the single largest structural break in Chilean public finance.

breaks.label: Decimal peso introduced
breaks.description: Chile decimalized its currency, replacing the colonial real-based system with a peso of 100 centavos. Pre-1851 fiscal series originate in reales and were converted to pesos at the source; conversions are not always documented per cell.
breaks.citation: Decreto sobre Monedas, 9 de enero de 1851; Banco Central de Chile, Historia Monetaria de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a thin vertical rule at 1851 on any nominal-peso series. Hover tooltip names the reform. Do not gray; the conversion is per-cell at the source.

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

breaks.label: Decimal peso introduced
breaks.description: Chile decimalized its currency, replacing the colonial real-based system with a peso of 100 centavos. Pre-1851 fiscal series originate in reales and were converted to pesos at the source; conversions are not always documented per cell.
breaks.citation: Decreto sobre Monedas, 9 de enero de 1851; Banco Central de Chile, Historia Monetaria de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a thin vertical rule at 1851 on any nominal-peso series. Hover tooltip names the reform. Do not gray; the conversion is per-cell at the source.

breaks.label: Central Bank founded; peso pegged to gold
breaks.description: The Kemmerer mission of 1925 created the Banco Central de Chile (Decree-Law 486, August 1925) and pegged the peso to gold at 6 pence sterling. Pre-1925 fiscal and monetary series are nominal-peso, post-1925 reflect the gold-standard regime through its 1932 abandonment.
breaks.citation: Decreto-Ley 486 de 1925, creación del Banco Central de Chile; Edwin W. Kemmerer (1925), Report on the Central Bank of Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a vertical rule at 1925; tooltip names Central Bank founding and the gold peg.

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

breaks.label: Tacna returned to Peru (Treaty of Lima)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Lima of June 3, 1929 settled the Tacna-Arica question: Tacna returned to Peru, Arica confirmed Chilean. National-aggregate series experience a small reduction in 1929; the Tacna department disappears from Chilean reporting after this date.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Lima, June 3, 1929; St. John (1992), The Bolivia–Chile–Peru Dispute.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1929 on national series with subnational composition. Department-level series for Tacna terminate in 1929 and should not be drawn beyond that year.

breaks.label: Anuario primary → later compiled official series
breaks.description: For long-run national series (GDP, fiscal aggregates, foreign trade, demographics), the pre-1929 segment is drawn from the primary archival series (Anuario Estadistico, Sinopsis, Memoria), while later years rely on subsequent official statistical series. Definitions were harmonized across the join and may differ slightly from the original primary readings.
breaks.citation: Primary Chilean statistical series (Anuario, Sinopsis, Memoria) and later official series.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Source caption attributes by year-segment per audit Finding 4.2. No vertical rule required unless a definitional revision crossed this date.

breaks.label: Decimal peso introduced
breaks.description: Chile decimalized its currency, replacing the colonial real-based system with a peso of 100 centavos. Pre-1851 fiscal series originate in reales and were converted to pesos at the source; conversions are not always documented per cell.
breaks.citation: Decreto sobre Monedas, 9 de enero de 1851; Banco Central de Chile, Historia Monetaria de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a thin vertical rule at 1851 on any nominal-peso series. Hover tooltip names the reform. Do not gray; the conversion is per-cell at the source.

breaks.label: Central Bank founded; peso pegged to gold
breaks.description: The Kemmerer mission of 1925 created the Banco Central de Chile (Decree-Law 486, August 1925) and pegged the peso to gold at 6 pence sterling. Pre-1925 fiscal and monetary series are nominal-peso, post-1925 reflect the gold-standard regime through its 1932 abandonment.
breaks.citation: Decreto-Ley 486 de 1925, creación del Banco Central de Chile; Edwin W. Kemmerer (1925), Report on the Central Bank of Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Draw a vertical rule at 1925; tooltip names Central Bank founding and the gold peg.

breaks.label: Tarapacá annexed (Treaty of Ancón)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Ancón (October 20, 1883) transferred Tarapacá Province from Peru to Chile. National-level population, fiscal-revenue, and saltpeter series jump because the territorial base grew; department- and province-level series are unaffected outside Tarapacá itself.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Ancón, October 20, 1883; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1883 on national-aggregate series. For department/province maps, Tarapacá appears in the data starting 1884 (1883 was a transition year); the choropleth should show this as new geography rather than missing data.

breaks.label: Antofagasta annexed (Pacto de Tregua)
breaks.description: The Pacto de Tregua of April 4, 1884 transferred Antofagasta from Bolivia to Chilean administration; the formal cession came with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. The 1884 pact is the working date for the data; Antofagasta enters Chilean statistical reporting from this year.
breaks.citation: Pacto de Tregua, 4 de abril de 1884; Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904; Sater (2007), Andean Tragedy.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1884. The pre-1883 baseline excludes both Tarapacá and Antofagasta and is the relevant comparison year for the new territories.

breaks.label: Tacna returned to Peru (Treaty of Lima)
breaks.description: The Treaty of Lima of June 3, 1929 settled the Tacna-Arica question: Tacna returned to Peru, Arica confirmed Chilean. National-aggregate series experience a small reduction in 1929; the Tacna department disappears from Chilean reporting after this date.
breaks.citation: Treaty of Lima, June 3, 1929; St. John (1992), The Bolivia–Chile–Peru Dispute.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Vertical rule at 1929 on national series with subnational composition. Department-level series for Tacna terminate in 1929 and should not be drawn beyond that year.

breaks.label: Anuario primary → later compiled official series
breaks.description: For long-run national series (GDP, fiscal aggregates, foreign trade, demographics), the pre-1929 segment is drawn from the primary archival series (Anuario Estadistico, Sinopsis, Memoria), while later years rely on subsequent official statistical series. Definitions were harmonized across the join and may differ slightly from the original primary readings.
breaks.citation: Primary Chilean statistical series (Anuario, Sinopsis, Memoria) and later official series.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Source caption attributes by year-segment per audit Finding 4.2. No vertical rule required unless a definitional revision crossed this date.

Series originating from INE after 1970 use modern definitions, including the 1976 labor-force survey redesign that breaks unemployment comparability with pre-1976 figures.

breaks.label: September 1973 — political rupture
breaks.description: The military government that took power on September 11, 1973 disrupted civilian statistical reporting for several years and introduced methodological changes in social and economic series. Fiscal, labor, and social-sector series across 1972–1976 are particularly affected by definitional turnover and, in some cases, political contestation of the published figures.
breaks.citation: Meller (2000); Ffrench-Davis (2001).
breaks.rule_for_chart: Light vertical rule at 1973 on long-run series. Tooltip notes the political-economic discontinuity without making a substantive judgment. Comparison across this break is methodologically legitimate but readers should know the regime change.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

breaks.label: CONARA regionalization (13 regions replace provinces)
breaks.description: Decreto-Ley 575 of July 1974, implemented through 1975-1976, replaced Chile's 25-province structure with 13 regions plus the Metropolitan Region. Department-level reporting effectively ends; from this date forward the canonical subnational geography is the region (XV regions today, after later subdivisions).
breaks.citation: Decreto-Ley 575 de 1974; ODEPLAN/CONARA (1976), Chile hacia un nuevo destino.
breaks.rule_for_chart: Department and province series should not be drawn past 1974 without a notice; the data after this date originates from region-level reporting back-cast to the older units, which is interpolation. Recommended: terminate department/province series at 1973 by default with an option to view the back-cast extension.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

definition: Marriages recorded in the 20 to 24 age band, 1964 to 1973, from Mamalakis's Historical Statistics of Chile. breaks.label: September 1973 — political rupture
breaks.description: The military government that took power on September 11, 1973 disrupted civilian statistical reporting for several years and introduced methodological changes in social and economic series. Fiscal, labor, and social-sector series across 1972–1976 are particularly affected by definitional turnover and, in some cases, political contestation of the published figures.
breaks.citation: Meller (2000); Ffrench-Davis (2001).
breaks.rule_for_chart: Light vertical rule at 1973 on long-run series. Tooltip notes the political-economic discontinuity without making a substantive judgment. Comparison across this break is methodologically legitimate but readers should know the regime change.

definition: Stillbirths registered in the year. Chile counted these separately from infant deaths, so the series complements rather than duplicates deaths under one year. Coverage is national from 1900 and subnational from the 1920s. Registration of a stillbirth was less complete than of a live birth throughout the period, so levels are understated and the trend is more reliable than any single year.

breaks.label: Provincial reorganization (DFL 8,582)
breaks.description: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 of 1927, in force 1928, redrew Chile's provincial map. Some 19th-century departments merged, new provinces were created from departmental groupings, and several department names persisted into different boundary contexts. The 52-panel that anchors this dataset is built from the pre-1928 frame; post-1928 departments map imperfectly to it.
breaks.citation: Decreto con Fuerza de Ley 8,582 de 1927; Cavieres (1988), División político-administrativa de Chile.
breaks.rule_for_chart: All department and province series should annotate 1928 as a boundary discontinuity. Cross-break comparisons of the same named department before and after 1928 are not on the same geography and should carry a notice. The platform's choice of 1920 as the last department GeoJSON frame predates this reform; users mapping post-1928 data onto pre-1928 geometry are looking at a fiction.

definition: Customs (external trade) duties as a percentage of total ordinary fiscal revenue. Computed by this project as revenue_customs_pesos divided by revenue_total_ordinary_pesos, times 100. Both inputs are PRIMARY per-ramo revenue levels in nominal pesos, transcribed from the Memorias de Hacienda and the Anuario Estadistico fiscal cuadros and reconciled to each source's printed total; the share therefore carries no secondary-compilation lineage. Coverage follows the extracted level years.
